Digital Rehab

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What does it take to recover from digital addiction and compulsive screen use? Carte Blanche shows what the law demands of parents and the cures that science has proven.

Summary:
The Collins dictionary's word of the year for 2015 is "bringe watching" -- with Netflix and Showmax coming on stream, it's a word that's likely to find more and more currency. How do we recover form compulsive digital consumption in permanently switched-on world? How do we remain in recovery for digital addiction if we depend so heavily on technology for legitimate uses like learning, work and entertainment? How do we wrest back control from media that has forced us into passivity and use it in pro-active ways in classrooms and at home?
We explore how two heavy users came to terms with their screen use as an addiction -- and the steps they took to recover. We examine the legal onus on parents and online media creators (like Whatsapp or Instagram) to build protections into their software and pro-actively prevent the vulnerable from developing process addiction and suggest ways in which to take back control of screens.

Press Release:


Digital Detox
Is your every move linked to a digital device, computer screen, or an app – a technological sub-culture that’s always with you? In a permanently switched-on world where compulsive digital consumption is the norm, Carte Blanche asks – what does it take to recover from tech addiction?


Script:


PROMOS:

FIFTEEN
CRAIG BLEWETT: We used to medicate them with chemical tablets, we’re now going to try and medicate them with silicone tablets.
VO: Is there still time to protect new users against the rise of internet addiction? Are we a generation in desperate need of digital detox?

FIFTEEN
NIC ADAMS: I realized the connection to ‘have to have my cell phone’, ‘have to have a laptop’…was actually controlling my life.
VO: Are your digital screen use habits getting away from you? Is it time to consider digital detox?

TEN
VO: Are your device screens the first and last things you see every day? Do you break into a cold sweat when your batteries run down? Could you be in need of digital detox?


STORY: DIGITAL DETOX
From around the world technology-weary souls flood to the Californian Redwoods and pay hundreds of dollars for a weekend of inner restoration and outer reconnection with people, face to face – not in texts.
Camp Grounded was started by burnt-out internet executives.
UPS CAMP GROUNDED VIDEO: You guys, you just got here, it’s important that we do things in the right order – it’s time for milk and cookies.
JOHN WEBB: Digital detox retreats are well established in the West, and even more so in Far East with military-style boot-camps for teenage video-gaming addicts, where governments have recognized internet addiction as the biggest threat against their youth. But the tech rehab trend has been slow to reach South African shores. When Namibian hotelier Nic Adams looked for help for his compulsive screen habit, he only found holistic detox retreats. Still, the promise of being stripped of his devices on arrival felt like what he needed.
JOHN WEBB: So you arrived in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands and you were exposed to this alien environment. Did it feel like one of your limbs had been chopped off?
NIC ADAMS: Television was taken out of the room, no cell phone, there was nothing – for a whole week. And I realized the connection to ‘have to have my cell phone’, ‘have to have a laptop’, ‘have to be with information’ was actually controlling my life. I was no longer in control of my life.
Last year our report DIGITAL COCAINE drew together the latest neuroscience equating the effects of extended digital task switching to the effects of cocaine on the brain. Cape Town Psychologist Andre le Roux specialises in addiction to processes. He sees a rising incidence of internet addiction, which often coincides with substance abuse and lots of denial.
ANDRE LE ROUX: It usually takes a crisis before people actually realize, so very often it’s a fight in the family. And then you find that when people are trying to cut down or do it less that they actually discover that they don’t have the control that they thought they had.
NIC ADAMS: I was bought up in the era where we didn’t even have television. So all of a sudden you’ve gotten more and more and more toys. It was almost like my cigarette addiction at the time – it was the first thing that you do in the morning. My body started telling me that things were not quite right. My lifestyle was not really where one would be happy.
ANDRE LE ROUX: Often the people around them also go into denial because they hear the blaming, the minimizing, the justifying. It’s one of the hardest addictions because you’re going to face it in your daily life.
DSM5, the Bible of Mental Disorders, says PROCESS addiction destroys lives in the same ways as drugs – the inability to feel normal without it; needing more to feel as good as at first; lying to conceal how much is used; conflict and destruction in relationships.
Friends have rated 20-year old film student Zaitoon Moses the most online person they know. A compulsive texter, she can’t bear to switch her phone to silent and chats while working.
ZAITOON: It even rings in class at times…my my grandmother actually always shouts, I should put it down, I should put it aside…
Filming on set means phones must be off – boundaries that are beginning to challenge Zaitoon’s screen use.
ZAITOON: I think I will be asking how does other people work while the cell phones are on…being in the industry has taught me you need to set boundaries for yourself.
JOHN: At what point should someone come and see you?
ANDRE LE ROUX: It’s like a wake up point of saying ‘why am I doing this’, ‘what’s it doing’, ‘what is really the meaning and purpose in this?’
NIC ADAMS: I looked at myself and I said, you know, ‘you’re not gonna last’. And I started looking around at detoxes.
For Nic a simple detox triggered an understanding of his issues and lifelong recovery – to this day, he takes analogue breaks. Work boundaries are challenging Zaitoon to think about her own use.
But for some, just as with substance abuse, proper rehab may be unavoidable.
ANDRE LE ROUX: Good and professional help is certainly available – 12 step support groups…
JOHN WEBB: My concern as a parent is how I control this process – when I see my very young child being so adept in the technological sphere that a lot of it is out of our control.
ANDRE LE ROUX: And that’s the key role really to teach people is what is normal, where are their boundaries, and where are some rules.
Technology in education specialist Dr Craig Blewett teaches ways to challenge addictive screen use.
CRAIG BLEWETT: You sleep seven hours a day…you spend nine hours a day on technology – you spend more time on your tech than sleeping…you’d rather not sleep.
With a PhD on the use of Facebook for learning, Craig trains schools to let kids CREATE, in stead of CONSUME.
JOHN WEBB: Do you sometimes feel that you’re fighting against time, because of new applications and new platforms are being developed all the time?
CRAIG BLEWETT: The Collins dictionary word of the year for last year was ‘binge-watching’. That basically refers to sitting in front of your TV, Netflix or whatever it is and watching an entire season. So the desire for people just to consume is getting bigger and bigger and bigger.
In 2007, the World Economic Forum ranked South Africa's global e-readiness at 47th – it’s dropped to 75th place last year.
JOHN LINK: So this year the Gauteng provincial government pioneered the “BIG SWITCH ON” to improve education and e-readiness. Saying that NO AMOUNT OF CRITICISM WOULD DETER them, Gauteng Education committed R17-billion over the next 5 years to make classrooms paperless. 
CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: We want you to succeed and we want to support you every inch of the way.
While we catch up on digital roll-out, Craig wants to see therapy applied before problems arise.
CRAIG BLEWETT: We have a problem with learners who are possibly hard to keep their attention. We used to medicate them with chemical tablets, we’re now going to try and medicate them with silicone tablets. And that’s not working. Simply putting technology in front of a learner and assuming they’re gonna know how to use it effectively, or even the teacher’s gonna know how to use it effectively – that’s not helping
JOHN WEBB: What exactly is ‘motivational enhancement therapy’?
CRAIG BLEWETT: Rather than taking addiction you rather focus on the positive side of things, you try and say ‘well where would we like to be’, ‘what would we like to be doing and what would we like to become?’ you create motivation the motivation is ‘imagine if you could have your own YouTube video, your own channel, would you like to do that? You’re creating motivations. At the end of the day when you’ve read 5000 posts, you don’t have anything. But when you’ve put in some energy to make something, it’s still there.
Ahead of the e-roll-out curve, Westville Girls High is clear on what should be put in place — alongside screens — to survive THE BIG SWITCH ON.
GIRL 1: My parents they limit where internet usage goes – facebook accounts, twitter accounts, I’m not allowed to have my phone probably one or two hours a day.
GIRL 2: When you’re active and you’re having fun and you’re moving then technology kinda like disappears.
MELISA EICHERT: As a mom and as a teacher, parents are scared of their children; they’re scared to say no to their 3-year-olds and they’re scared to say no to their 14-year-olds. So it is going to be a problem, yes, there is an addiction. walk into a supermarket and kind are screaming in the trolley; what do moms do? They hand them the cell phone and they swipe and they play with the phone and they’re happy. It’s what’s going to happen when that child gets to 13 or 14?
Peter Strasheim, an attorney specializing in medical law, psychology and social justice says process addiction is becoming so serious that devices and apps may soon be compelled to come with warnings or auto-shutdown.
PETER STRASHEIM: You would reasonably expect the regulator in the industry to start saying that software is built into them, into the device, to detect that this person is now using the phone at 3 or 4 in the morning. And if they can discern from algorithms, that their age is now 14-years-old, that would be a risk to the user.
CRAIG BLEWETT: There is some quite clever software that is around that allows you to limit and control the amount of time your children are spending online, but they’re not the solution. My worry is when we put those things in, we think well I’ve dealt with it, the kids are ok. Concerned parents doing things in the right ways, concerned teachers, is the solutions to these things.
Strasheim says the Constitution and Equality Laws place a far greater onus on parents to act than they may be aware.
PETER STRASHEIM: A parent who buys the phone needs, under the Children’s Act, to make sure that they act in the best interests of the child and the constitutional rights of the child. One of those will be certainly to make sure that the child hasn’t become so process addicted to the phone that their sleep patterns are affected, their interpersonal psychological skills are not affected and that they get enough sleep to function correctly and appropriately at school. It’s possible that if a parent didn’t take the necessary steps when they had reason to believe their child was acting inappropriately or using their phone excessively, and if their psychological health was affected, the child could potentially bring some sort of discrimination claim under the Equality Act against the parent for not acting when the parent knew…
ANDRE LE ROUX: There’s a process of needing to learn some of the root causes and even some of the life skills that people actually need to bring in place of those old behaviours. After a while it’s not about the not using anymore, but it’s about the starting to live – live without the obsession, the compulsion.
JOHN WEBB: How did the course change your life?
NIC ADAMS: It made a massive difference in my life…You were, for once, you were in control of your own life.
